setupSteps: Choose the weight. Start with the lightest option that lets you do 10 clean slow reps with 3-4 reps left in the tank (see section 7). If you are new, the first session can be a bodyweight squat with the hands clasped at the chest.
Mat. A non-slip mat on a flat spot; clear 1 m x 1 m. Put a folded towel or a second mat beside you to set the weight down on.

Chair or box (optional, recommended for week 1). Place a sturdy chair, stool or box behind you so that its seat is at about knee height (a seat height of about 40-45 cm suits most adults, est.). The chair must not slide: put its back against a wall.
Pick the weight up safely. Bend the knees and hips to lift it from the floor (a mini squat), do not round the back to pick it up.

Hold position. Dumbbell: stand it vertically and hold the top end with both hands cupped under the upper head. Kettlebell: grip the horns or the sides of the handle with the bell hanging down. Rucksack: hug it to the chest by the top handle or both arms. Water bottle: both hands around the bottle at the sternum. Hold the weight against the breastbone with the elbows pointing down and slightly in front of the ribs.

Stance. Feet about shoulder-width apart (sources describe a stance between hip-width and a bit wider than the shoulders, with the toes turned out about 15-30 degrees, est.; the exact numbers vary, so use the width where your knees and hips feel free at depth). If you cannot get deep, try slightly wider and more turned out.
Stand tall. Ears over shoulders over hips; chest proud (not leaned back), ribs down over the hips, gaze forward at a spot on the wall at eye level.

Heels. Feet flat; if your heels lift in the squat, put a small stable plate or flat book under each heel (0.5-2 cm; sources vary from about 1.3 to 5 cm for the lift, est.) and work on ankle mobility between sessions (Fit&Well, Human Kinetics, snippets).
Camera. Phone in landscape at about hip height (80-100 cm, est.), 2-2.5 m to the side (side view), full body from head to floor in frame.
Warm up 3-5 minutes (est.): march on the spot, hip circles, 5-8 bodyweight squats (Home 1), a few arm circles, and one or two light goblet squats with a lighter object.

steps.title: Stand tall with the weight at your chest
steps.action: Feet shoulder-width, toes turned out slightly, weight held against the breastbone, elbows pointing down.
steps.feel: Weight light against the chest, shoulders relaxed, belly gently firm.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ear, shoulder, hip and ankle roughly in one line; the weight touches the chest. Front: shoulders level, feet even.

steps.title: Brace
steps.action: Lightly tighten the tummy as if about to be tapped, ribs down.
steps.feel: A firm trunk, not a held breath.
steps.breathing: A comfortable breath in; do not hold it for the whole rep.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ribs not flared, lower back neutral (not hollowed).

steps.title: Start sitting down: hips and knees bend together
steps.action: Push the hips back and bend the knees at the same time, as if sitting into a chair.
steps.feel: Weight spread across the whole foot, thighs working.
steps.visualCheck: Side: shins lean forward and the torso leans only a little; the knees travel forward in line with the toes. Front: knees track over the 2nd-3rd toe.

steps.title: Keep the chest tall and the elbows low
steps.action: As you lower, keep the chest up and the weight against the chest; let the elbows move down between the knees.
steps.feel: Tall spine, a slight stretch in the inner thighs and hips.
steps.visualCheck: Side: spine stays in one line (no rounding). Front: elbows approach the inside of the knees; the common cue is elbows to inside of knees, which also pushes the knees out (coaching sources).

steps.title: Reach a comfortable depth
steps.action: Go down until the thighs are about parallel to the floor or as deep as you can while the heels stay flat and the back stays straight. Many guides use parallel or hips just below the knees; ACE's listing says continue lowering until the hips drop below the knees (snippet). For a beginner, box or chair height is the depth target. Prioritise form over depth.
steps.feel: Strong thighs and bottom, heels pressing down, no pinching in the front of the hips.
steps.visualCheck: Side: thighs about parallel (knee angle roughly 80-100 degrees, est.); heels flat; torso still tall. Front: knees over the toes, not caving in; feet flat.

steps.title: Press the floor away and stand
steps.action: Push through the whole foot, keep the chest tall, and drive the hips and knees up together.
steps.feel: Thighs and bottom pushing; the weight stays at the chest.
steps.breathing: Breathe out as you stand (do not hold the breath).
steps.visualCheck: Side: hips do not shoot up first; the torso angle stays about the same. Front: knees stay in line with the toes.

steps.title: Finish tall
steps.action: Stand straight, hips under shoulders, squeeze the bottom gently; do not lean back.
steps.feel: Tall and balanced; a calm bottom squeeze.
steps.breathing: Breathe in for the next rep.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ears over shoulders over hips; knees extended but not locked back. Front: weight still centred at the chest.

steps.title: Set the weight down safely
steps.action: After the last rep, bend the knees and hips and place the weight gently on the towel or mat, with a 2-3 s lowering count.
steps.visualCheck: Side: back neutral; no drop. The only sound should be a soft touch.

commonMistakes.title: Letting the weight drift away from the chest
commonMistakes.text: Letting the weight drift away from the chest. Why: the load pulls you forward and the counterbalance benefit is lost (coaching source in snippets). Fix: hug the weight to the breastbone, elbows down.

commonMistakes.title: Rounding the back at the bottom
commonMistakes.text: Rounding the back at the bottom. Why: the trunk loses its brace and loads the lower back. Fix: stop at a depth where the spine stays straight (use a box or chair target), keep the chest proud and the ribs down.

commonMistakes.title: Heels lifting
commonMistakes.text: Heels lifting. Why: tight ankles shift weight to the toes and tip you forward. Fix: a small stable plate or flat book under the heels, slower reps, ankle mobility work between sessions; reduce plate height as the ankle improves (Human Kinetics, Fit&Well, snippets).

commonMistakes.title: Knees caving in
commonMistakes.text: Knees caving in. Why: dynamic knee valgus is widely treated as a risk factor for knee injuries, although some studies are contradictory (narrative reviews, snippets). Fix: elbows push the knees out, feet turned out slightly, lighter weight, and front-view video check; a band above the knees is a cue some coaches use, but one barbell study found it increased valgus, so do not rely on it.

commonMistakes.title: Hips shooting up first
commonMistakes.text: Hips shooting up first. Why: turns the squat into a good-morning, loading the back instead of the thighs. Fix: slower ascent, "chest up and hips up together", lighter weight.

commonMistakes.title: Dropping too fast and bouncing
commonMistakes.text: Dropping too fast and bouncing. Why: loses control and adds noise on the floor below. Fix: 3 s lowering count, 1 s pause at the bottom, and press up smoothly.

commonMistakes.title: Chasing depth with a rounded back
commonMistakes.text: Chasing depth with a rounded back. Why: a "butt wink" (tucking of the pelvis) at the bottom puts load on the spine. Fix: stop where the back stays straight; use the box depth; depth comes with practice.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Why: raises blood pressure and brings dizziness (breathing study PubMed 7741618, carried from earlier items). Fix: breathe in on the way down, out on the way up.

commonMistakes.title: Too heavy too soon
commonMistakes.text: Too heavy too soon. Why: form fails by rep 4-5. Fix: use 3-4 reps in reserve; the last rep should look like the first.

commonMistakes.title: Wobbly chair or sliding box
commonMistakes.text: Wobbly chair or sliding box. Why: a collapse onto the seat jars the spine. Fix: back the chair against a wall, sit lightly and stand, do not drop onto it.

safetyNotes: Knee problems: use the box or chair, a partial range, light load; keep pain low; a clinic guideline lists half squats and wall squats for moderate knee osteoarthritis, with changes by the clinician (Sanford Health, snippet). One physiotherapy programme caps pain at 4/10 (Pure Physiotherapy, snippet); that is one clinic's rule, not a general standard.
Lower back problems: use a light weight, stay tall, keep the box, and stop if pain spreads down a leg or is sharp.
Shoulder problems: the goblet hold is a low-demand grip, but if holding the weight at the chest hurts, use the bodyweight squat with the arms crossed or a lighter object hugged to the chest.

High blood pressure and heart disease: breathe out as you stand; do not hold the breath; use light weights and moderate effort; get medical clearance first if you have heart disease or uncontrolled blood pressure.

Osteoporosis: strength training is generally recommended; avoid loaded rounding or twisting of the spine, and with severe osteoporosis or a prior vertebral fracture ask a clinician first (reviews, snippets).

Pregnancy and postpartum: squats are commonly used, but ask your obstetrician, midwife or women's health physiotherapist; stop with pelvic heaviness, leaking or pain; box squats and lighter loads are typical modifications.
Mumbai flat: put the weight down gently, on a mat or towel, with a controlled lowering count; do not drop a dumbbell on a tile floor; avoid the balcony slab.
